meta.title: Who really said "Never put off till tomorrow what may be done day after tomorrow just as well"? | Quotle.info
meta.description: Yes — Mark Twain wrote it, as a joke fake-Franklin maxim in his 1870 essay “The Late Benjamin Franklin.” He even signed it ‘B. F.’
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'Never put off till tomorrow what may be done day after tomorrow just as well'?
meta.ogDescription: Mark Twain coined it in 1870 as a satirical fake-Franklin maxim — signed ‘B. F.’ The popular wording lightly refines his original.

answer.label: Written by
answer.authorDates: 1835–1910 · American author and humorist; written when he was 34
answer.sourceLine: Twain coined it as a mock “Benjamin Franklin” maxim to open his satirical essay “The Late Benjamin Franklin” ↗ in The Galaxy (July 1870), signing it “B. F.” His original reads “what you can do day after to-morrow”; the widely quoted “what may be done” is a later refinement of the same line.

source.heading: Where it really comes from
source.excerpt: Never put off till to-morrow what you can do day after to-morrow just as well.—B. F.
trail: The straight proverb — “never put off till to-morrow what you can do to-day” — was popularized in the Earl of Chesterfield’s letters to his son (written from 1737, published 1774) ↗.
In July 1870 Mark Twain inverted it in “The Late Benjamin Franklin,” The Galaxy ↗, printing “Never put off till to-morrow what you can do day after to-morrow just as well” and signing it “B. F.”
Per Quote Investigator ↗, later reprintings smoothed the grammar (adding “the” and shifting to “may be done”), which is how the modern popular wording arose.
source.cutTag: ↑ Twain’s original wording — the popular version swaps in “what may be done”
source.excerptNote: Twain opened the essay with this fake Franklin aphorism and then mock-lamented how Franklin’s “maxims” had tortured generations of boys. The “B. F.” signature is the joke: the sentiment is the exact opposite of Franklin’s real thrift-and-industry counsel.

author.name: Mark Twain
author.heading: About Mark Twain
author.bio: Mark Twain was the pen name of Samuel Langhorne Clemens (1835–1910), the American humorist and novelist behind The Adventures of Tom Sawyer and Adventures of Huckleberry Finn. A relentless parodist of Victorian self-improvement piety, he loved to invert earnest maxims — here targeting the near-sacred aphorisms of Benjamin Franklin. The upside-down proverb is characteristic Twain: it reads like folk wisdom while gently mocking the whole genre of it.

misattribution.heading: Who it’s wrongly credited to
misattribution.intro: Because Twain signed his joke “B. F.,” the line is sometimes repeated as if Benjamin Franklin actually wrote it — and a mid-century biography handed it to Oscar Wilde.

items.why: Twain invented the maxim and signed it “B. F.” as satire; it is the reverse of Franklin’s real thrift-and-diligence counsel. Franklin never wrote it — per Quote Investigator ↗, the phrasing was Twain’s 1870 parody of Franklin.
Hesketh Pearson’s 1946 biography of Wilde presented the quip as Wilde’s, but no instance predating that book has been found ↗ — and Twain’s printed version predates Wilde’s writing career.

misattribution.truthLine: The words are genuinely Mark Twain’s, first printed in “The Late Benjamin Franklin,” The Galaxy, July 1870 ↗.

context.heading: Why it caught on
lead: The joke works because it wears the costume of a real proverb. The straight maxim — “Never put off till to-morrow what you can do to-day” — was already a household scold, popularized in the Earl of Chesterfield’s letters to his son (written from 1737, published 1774). Twain simply pushed the timeline one day further and let procrastination win.

Attaching it to “B. F.” sharpened the satire: Benjamin Franklin was the patron saint of American industriousness, so a lazy maxim in his name was a small act of literary vandalism — and exactly the kind of thing Twain built a career on.
context.pull: Twain didn’t misquote Franklin. He forged him — on purpose, for laughs.
